newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tennis star Graf's father enjoyed lavish lifestyle.
newsitem.headline: Tennis star Graf's father enjoyed lavish lifestyle.

text.p: Peter Graf is a former second-hand car salesman who enjoyed a lavish lifestyle after he taught his daughter to hit a tennis ball over a net for money.
On Friday the 58-year-old was just happy to use his two feet to walk away from prison guards.

Some 15 months of imprisonment came to an end when a German court decided that the father of the world's best female tennis player Steffi Graf could be released on bail while his trial for allegedly evading millions of marks (dollars) in tax continues.

For a man used to wining and dining with the VIPs of sport and politics, prison provided a sobering and solitary existence for Graf as he pondered over the way he has managed Germany's most popular sports star for the last two decades.
"I want to be at home," Graf said simply after shaking hands with his lawyers and slipping out the back door of a Mannheim courtroom.
A car was waiting to drive him to his home in nearby Bruehl, of course. But it was nothing fancy -- just an ordinary brown saloon car, the kind he used to sell before Steffi came along.
Most daughters have a special relationship with their father. But for Steffi, who first picked up a tennis racket as a three-year-old, Peter Graf dominated her life.
Graf first started tuning her forehand by battering a ball against the wall for hours in a room in the cellar at home.

She was obsessed with the game, her father said, and at six, she won her first tournament. Two years later Peter gave up his job, leased an indoor tennis court and concentrated all his time on managing her affairs.
Until Graf was arrested in August last year after tax officials raided their homes, the two had virtually been inseparable.

In the early part of her career Peter organised her training, education and marketing. Later he sat in the stands to provide moral support at major tournaments and struck deals with businessmen in tennis's ubiquitous VIP tents.

He turned Steffi into the most marketable sportswoman in Germany, advertising everything from pasta to deodorant. Now the way he handled the millions that came from the sponsors and tournaments has come under the microscope.
Steffi, 27, says she knew little about the money she earned. Even when she won a tournament, she had nothing to do with the prize money.
"It is not normal that I go and get the cheque. It is my father or someone else who is asked to deal with it," she said.
There were times when Steffi was advised by some of her rivals to enjoy more independence from her father.
While Steffi owes a lot to her father, she has also suffered emotionally because of his actions in the past.
In 1990 her form dipped when stories of Peter's relationship with a topless model were splashed all over the German newspapers.
Although she has performed remarkably well in the last 15 months, Steffi has broken down several times in public when asked about the pressure of the tax affair.
Peter Graf still has a long way to go before he can walk free. He is accused of evading 19 million marks ($13 million) of tax on his daughter's earnings between 1989 and 1993.
His mental health has been the subject of a great deal of speculation in the German newspapers. He will have to report to police twice a week and receive pyschotherapy.
